Posterior predictive check for a false-positive occupancy model

Source: R/fp_ppc.R
fp_ppc.Rd

Replicates the detection data from the posterior of an fp_occu() fit and compares observed and replicated data with a discrepancy statistic, giving a Bayesian p-value. Detections are summed per site, so the check asks whether the model reproduces how many detections each site gets.

Usage

fp_ppc(
  object,
  method = c("automated", "verified"),
  fit_stat = c("freeman-tukey", "chi-squared"),
  ndraws = 1000,
  seed = NULL
)

Arguments

object

An fp_occu object.

method

Which data to check: "automated" (default; every site) or "verified" (verified sites only).

fit_stat

Discrepancy statistic: "freeman-tukey" (default), \(\sum_i (\sqrt{y_i} - \sqrt{E_i})^2\), or "chi-squared", \(\sum_i (y_i - E_i)^2 / E_i\), where \(y_i\) is the number of detections at site \(i\) and \(E_i\) its expected value given the parameters and the latent state.

ndraws

Number of posterior draws to use, sampled without replacement. NULL uses all of them.

seed

Optional integer seed for the subsampling and replication.

Value

An object of class fp_ppc, a list with y (observed detections per site), yrep (matrix of replicated detections, draws in rows and sites in columns), fit_obs and fit_rep (discrepancy of the observed and replicated data, one value per draw), p_value, site (the site identifiers of the columns), method, and fit_stat.

Details

The latent occupancy state is marginalized in the Stan model, so for each posterior draw \(z_i\) is first drawn from its conditional posterior given the data and the parameters, $$\Pr(z_i = 1 \mid \mathbf{y}_i, \theta) = \frac{\psi_i\, f(\mathbf{y}_i \mid z_i = 1, \theta)}{\psi_i\, f(\mathbf{y}_i \mid z_i = 1, \theta) + (1 - \psi_i)\, f(\mathbf{y}_i \mid z_i = 0, \theta)},$$ which is 1 at sites with a verified detection. Given \(z_i\), automated detections are replicated with probability \(z_i p_{11} + (1 - z_i) p_{10}\) and verified detections with probability \(z_i r_{11}\). The discrepancy is computed for the observed and the replicated data with the same \(z\) and parameters, and the Bayesian p-value is the proportion of draws in which the replicated discrepancy exceeds the observed one. Values near 0 or 1 indicate lack of fit; values near 0.5 indicate that the observed data are typical of the fitted model.

Under the observation-confirmation design, the conditional probability of \(z_i\) also uses the confirmed occasions, and "automated" checks the occasions that were not confirmed.

A p-value near 0.5 does not show that the false-positive process is correctly specified: a check of detection counts can have little power against a false-positive rate that tracks an unmeasured gradient. Use fp_calibrate() to ask whether the intervals of a given model are calibrated for a design.

The elements y and yrep follow the conventions of the 'bayesplot' package, so its ppc_*() functions can be used directly, for example bayesplot::ppc_bars(ppc$y, ppc$yrep).

See also

fp_occu(), fp_calibrate()

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
sim <- simulate_fp(nsite = 200, nocc = 10, seed = 1)
m <- fp_occu(sim$data, occ = ~ x, fp = ~ 1, random_recorder = FALSE)
ppc <- fp_ppc(m, ndraws = 500, seed = 1)
ppc
bayesplot::ppc_bars(ppc$y, ppc$yrep)
} # }
